extracted.intended_audience: USPTO rulewriters, patent practitioners, agency counsel, and public commenters on patent rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or drafting comments and analysis of USPTO Notices of Proposed Rulemaking under administrative law and related statutes (e.g., Paperwork Reduction Act, Information Quality Act, Executive Order 12,866). Focuses on disclosure, burden estimation, regulatory impact analysis, and procedural requirements for patent-regulatory rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper classification of regulations (interpretative vs legislative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation promulgated pursuant to a delegation of regulatory authority from Congress, using notice and comment procedure, will generally be classified as 'legislative' rather than 'interpretative.' The 'interpretative' exclusion does not apply to these regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases such as Nigro v. Sullivan and Chevron; exceptions include ultra vires provisions. Agencies should not characterize rules as interpretative to avoid notice-and-comment or enforcement consequences; IEEE-USA believes characterization as 'interpretive' is error here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of notice-and-comment for procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When promulgating procedural rules pursuant to authority in statutes like 35 U.S.C. §2(b)(2), the USPTO must engage in notice and comment rulemaking rather than claiming exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tafas/Tafas v. Kappos and related district court holdings bind the USPTO by its prior stipulation; Cooper Techs. dictum cannot be used to avoid the obligation. If the PTO believes Tafas does not apply it must explicitly state and justify a legal theory distinguishing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure of material facts and supporting evidence in the NPRM
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must disclose all material facts in the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and make its evidence available in a publicly-available rulemaking file at the time of the NPRM so the public has fair notice and meaningful opportunity to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure includes statistics, mathematical or computer models, and assumptions. Agencies must explain the assumptions and methodology used in preparing models and provide a complete analytic defense if models are challenged. See Connecticut Light & Power, Engine Mfrs’ Ass’n, Solite Corp., Small Refiner Lead Phase-Down Task Force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary or high-level information is insufficient without underlying data/models
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level summaries do not satisfy the disclosure duty; agencies must provide underlying models, data, and assumptions in intelligible form to allow meaningful public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washington Trollers, Chamber of Commerce v. SEC, and other precedents vacate rules where agencies relied on undisclosed extra-record materials or failed to provide the underlying model or data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act: consult public on burden methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Paperwork Reduction Act and implementing regs, the agency must consult with the public to solicit comment to 'evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 5 C.F.R. §1320.8(d)(1) and related PRA requirements; burden must include total time, effort, and financial resources expended by persons to generate, maintain, retain, or disclose information (44 U.S.C. §3502(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12,866: assess costs, benefits, and use best available information
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies shall assess both the costs and the benefits of the intended regulation and base decisions on the best reasonably obtainable scientific, technical, economic, and other information concerning the need for, and consequences of, the intended regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information required by EO 12,866 should be made available contemporaneously with the NPRM on the agency website per the E-Government Act. Agencies must quantify costs where feasible and explain consistency with statutory mandates and Presidential priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an integral, timely public rulemaking record
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must maintain a proper rulemaking record and make it timely available to the public during the notice-and-comment period; assembling a record only after litigation is improper and may render the rule invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanover Potato Products v. Shalala requires a contemporaneous record; courts will award fees and find rules arbitrary and capricious when the record is incomplete or produced only after suit. The public need not 'ferret out' missing documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose and justify numerical estimates and account for sample bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM must disclose the basis for numerical estimates (e.g., judge hours, number of petitions) and explain methodology; agencies must account for sample bias where present (e.g., using only completed reexaminations biases estimates downward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: USPTO's '98.7 hours of judge time' requires underlying data; failure to disclose estimation methodology undermines ability to reproduce or vet conclusions. Information Quality Act requires correction for sample bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide spreadsheets/models used for projections and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any spreadsheets or other models used to project growth, filing rates, or burden must be disclosed to allow independent reproduction and vetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PRA clearances span multi-year windows, burden projections must be reproducible (e.g., up through FY2015 in this context) and conform to agency Information Quality Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose distributional claim information and fee-category assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must disclose the distribution of claims per patent and how fee-category assignments were derived; aggregated tables without underlying claim distributions are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example criticism: table claiming all petitions fall into lowest fee category without claim-distribution data is not independently reproducible; economically significant patents tend to have more claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a broad set of economic impacts in regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking analyses must consider time costs of inventors and management, business disruption, settlement/arbitration costs, effects on investment (VC and angel), new business formation, and employment—i.e., the full range of economic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These effects are cognizable under the Paperwork Reduction Act, Regulatory Flexibility Act, and Executive Order 12,866 and are required by the America Invents Act (35 U.S.C. §§316(b), 326(b)) to consider effects on the economy and patent system integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economically significant rules require a Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rule may have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more, or otherwise raise novel legal or policy issues, it is 'economically significant' under EO 12,866 and requires a full Regulatory Impact Analysis including costs, benefits, and reasonably feasible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA should follow OMB Circular A-4 and include quantification of costs and benefits where feasible, assessment of alternatives, and an explanation why the chosen action is preferable. Agencies may not manipulate or 'credit' unrelated reductions to avoid the $100M threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act: burden estimates must be 'specific, objectively supported'
rubrics_metrics.description: PRA requires agencies to provide a specific, objectively supported estimate of burden for information collections; estimates must be transparent and reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 44 U.S.C. §3506(c)(1)(A)(iv). Prior USPTO estimates cited as too low and non-transparent; agencies should not rely on unsupported assumptions or opaque methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate proxies and consistent estimation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: When using proxies (e.g., inter partes reexamination to estimate AIA post-grant review filings), agencies must justify the proxy, adjust for known differences, and avoid internal inconsistencies (e.g., inconsistent counts between small-entity and total estimates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide objective derivation (e.g., empirical ratios from court decisions), include year-on-year growth projections over multi-year PRA windows, and reconcile seemingly conflicting statements in the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include full 'burden' not just attorney time when estimating paperwork costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperwork 'burden' includes attorney time, inventor and management time, client time, and other costs such as settlement negotiation or arbitration-related time—agencies must include full burden, not just attorney hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 5 C.F.R. §1320.3(b)(1) implementing 44 U.S.C. §3502(2); example: USPTO's estimate that a request to treat a settlement as confidential takes two hours ignores upstream settlement/negotiation burdens, understating true burden by orders of magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to significant public comments and address prior legal positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must fairly consider and respond to significant points raised by the public in comments and should not ignore legal issues raised previously (e.g., Tafas-related issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Home Box Office v. FCC and Kennecott v. EPA emphasize that opportunity to comment is meaningless unless agency responds to significant points; if the PTO disputes prior holdings it must state a reasoned legal defense rather than ignore them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on undisclosed extra-record materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may not base rules on materials not included in the public rulemaking record; reliance on undisclosed extra-record materials can lead to vacatur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chamber of Commerce v. SEC and related cases show courts vacate rules where agencies relied on undisclosed materials; all technical bases must be disclosed in time for meaningful commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow proposed disclosure ground rules (e.g., proposed §42.65(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO should consider and adopt its own proposed ground rules for disclosure (such as those in proposed §42.65(b)) as useful standards for agency transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IEEE-USA specifically recommends the USPTO follow its own proposed disclosure provisions as benchmarks for adequate disclosure in the NPRM and docket.
